section.title: Part 2: The Army on the March & Terrain
section.title_urdu: حصہ دوم: فوج کی پیش قدمی اور میدانِ جنگ

chapters.title: IX. THE ARMY ON THE MARCH
chapters.title_urdu: حصہ نہم: فوج کی پیش قدمی

paragraphs.text: 1. Sun Tzŭ said: We come now to the question of encamping the army, and observing signs of the enemy. Pass quickly over mountains, and keep in the neighbourhood of valleys.

sentences.text: Sun Tzŭ said: We come now to the question of encamping the army, and observing signs of the enemy.
Pass quickly over mountains, and keep in the neighbourhood of valleys.

paragraphs.text: 2. Camp in high places, facing the sun. Do not climb heights in order to fight. So much for mountain warfare.

sentences.text: Camp in high places, facing the sun.
Do not climb heights in order to fight.
So much for mountain warfare.

paragraphs.text: 3. After crossing a river, you should get far away from it.

sentences.text: After crossing a river, you should get far away from it.

paragraphs.text: 4. When an invading force crosses a river in its onward march, do not advance to meet it in mid-stream. It will be best to let half the army get across, and then deliver your attack.

sentences.text: When an invading force crosses a river in its onward march, do not advance to meet it in mid-stream.
It will be best to let half the army get across, and then deliver your attack.

paragraphs.text: 5. If you are anxious to fight, you should not go to meet the invader near a river which he has to cross.

sentences.text: If you are anxious to fight, you should not go to meet the invader near a river which he has to cross.

paragraphs.text: 6. Moor your craft higher up than the enemy, and facing the sun. Do not move up-stream to meet the enemy. So much for river warfare.

sentences.text: Moor your craft higher up than the enemy, and facing the sun.
Do not move up-stream to meet the enemy.
So much for river warfare.

paragraphs.text: 7. In crossing salt-marshes, your sole concern should be to get over them quickly, without any delay.

sentences.text: In crossing salt-marshes, your sole concern should be to get over them quickly, without any delay.

paragraphs.text: 8. If forced to fight in a salt-marsh, you should have water and grass near you, and get your back to a clump of trees. So much for operations in salt-marshes.

sentences.text: If forced to fight in a salt-marsh, you should have water and grass near you, and get your back to a clump of trees.
So much for operations in salt-marshes.

paragraphs.text: 9. In dry, level country, take up an easily accessible position with rising ground to your right and on your rear, so that the danger may be in front, and safety lie behind. So much for campaigning in flat country.

sentences.text: In dry, level country, take up an easily accessible position with rising ground to your right and on your rear, so that the danger may be in front, and safety lie behind.
So much for campaigning in flat country.

paragraphs.text: 10. These are the four useful branches of military knowledge which enabled the Yellow Emperor to vanquish four several sovereigns.

sentences.text: These are the four useful branches of military knowledge which enabled the Yellow Emperor to vanquish four several sovereigns.

paragraphs.text: 11. All armies prefer high ground to low, and sunny places to dark.

sentences.text: All armies prefer high ground to low, and sunny places to dark.

paragraphs.text: 12. If you are careful of your men, and camp on hard ground, the army will be free from disease of every kind, and this will spell victory.

sentences.text: If you are careful of your men, and camp on hard ground, the army will be free from disease of every kind, and this will spell victory.

paragraphs.text: 13. When you come to a hill or a bank, occupy the sunny side, with the slope on your right rear. Thus you will at once act for the benefit of your soldiers and utilise the natural advantages of the ground.

sentences.text: When you come to a hill or a bank, occupy the sunny side, with the slope on your right rear.
Thus you will at once act for the benefit of your soldiers and utilise the natural advantages of the ground.

paragraphs.text: 14. When, in consequence of heavy rains up-country, a river which you wish to ford is swollen and flecked with foam, you must wait until it subsides.

sentences.text: When, in consequence of heavy rains up-country, a river which you wish to ford is swollen and flecked with foam, you must wait until it subsides.

paragraphs.text: 15. Country in which there are precipitous cliffs with torrents running between, deep natural hollows, confined places, tangled thickets, quagmires and crevasses, should be left with all possible speed and not approached.

sentences.text: Country in which there are precipitous cliffs with torrents running between, deep natural hollows, confined places, tangled thickets, quagmires and crevasses, should be left with all possible speed and not approached.

paragraphs.text: 16. While we keep away from such places, we should get the enemy to approach them; while we face them, we should let the enemy have them on his rear.

sentences.text: While we keep away from such places, we should get the enemy to approach them; while we face them, we should let the enemy have them on his rear.

paragraphs.text: 17. If in the neighbourhood of your camp there should be any hilly country, ponds surrounded by aquatic grass, hollow basins filled with reeds, or woods with thick undergrowth, they must be carefully routed out and searched; for these are places where men in ambush or insidious spies are likely to be lurking.

sentences.text: If in the neighbourhood of your camp there should be any hilly country, ponds surrounded by aquatic grass, hollow basins filled with reeds, or woods with thick undergrowth, they must be carefully routed out and searched; for these are places where men in ambush or insidious spies are likely to be lurking.

paragraphs.text: 18. When the enemy is close at hand and remains quiet, he is relying on the natural strength of his position.

sentences.text: When the enemy is close at hand and remains quiet, he is relying on the natural strength of his position.

paragraphs.text: 19. When he keeps aloof and tries to provoke a battle, he is anxious for the other side to advance.

sentences.text: When he keeps aloof and tries to provoke a battle, he is anxious for the other side to advance.

paragraphs.text: 20. If his place of encampment is easy of access, he is tendering a bait.

sentences.text: If his place of encampment is easy of access, he is tendering a bait.

paragraphs.text: 21. Movement amongst the trees of a forest shows that the enemy is advancing. The appearance of a number of screens in the midst of thick grass means that the enemy wants to make us suspicious.

sentences.text: Movement amongst the trees of a forest shows that the enemy is advancing.
The appearance of a number of screens in the midst of thick grass means that the enemy wants to make us suspicious.

paragraphs.text: 22. The rising of birds in their flight is the sign of an ambuscade. Startled beasts indicate that a sudden attack is coming.

sentences.text: The rising of birds in their flight is the sign of an ambuscade.
Startled beasts indicate that a sudden attack is coming.

paragraphs.text: 23. When there is dust rising in a high column, it is the sign of chariots advancing; when the dust is low, but spread over a wide area, it betokens the approach of infantry. When it branches out in different directions, it shows that parties have been sent to collect firewood. A few clouds of dust moving to and fro signify that the army is encamping.

sentences.text: When there is dust rising in a high column, it is the sign of chariots advancing; when the dust is low, but spread over a wide area, it betokens the approach of infantry.
When it branches out in different directions, it shows that parties have been sent to collect firewood.
A few clouds of dust moving to and fro signify that the army is encamping.

paragraphs.text: 24. Humble words and increased preparations are signs that the enemy is about to advance. Violent language and driving forward as if to the attack are signs that he will retreat.

sentences.text: Humble words and increased preparations are signs that the enemy is about to advance.
Violent language and driving forward as if to the attack are signs that he will retreat.

paragraphs.text: 25. When the light chariots come out first and take up a position on the wings, it is a sign that the enemy is forming for battle.

sentences.text: When the light chariots come out first and take up a position on the wings, it is a sign that the enemy is forming for battle.

paragraphs.text: 26. Peace proposals unaccompanied by a sworn covenant indicate a plot.

sentences.text: Peace proposals unaccompanied by a sworn covenant indicate a plot.

paragraphs.text: 27. When there is much running about and the soldiers fall into rank, it means that the critical moment has come.

sentences.text: When there is much running about and the soldiers fall into rank, it means that the critical moment has come.

paragraphs.text: 28. When some are seen advancing and some retreating, it is a lure.

sentences.text: When some are seen advancing and some retreating, it is a lure.

paragraphs.text: 29. When the soldiers stand leaning on their spears, they are faint from want of food.

sentences.text: When the soldiers stand leaning on their spears, they are faint from want of food.

paragraphs.text: 30. If those who are sent to draw water begin by drinking themselves, the army is suffering from thirst.

sentences.text: If those who are sent to draw water begin by drinking themselves, the army is suffering from thirst.

paragraphs.text: 31. If the enemy sees an advantage to be gained and makes no effort to secure it, the soldiers are exhausted.

sentences.text: If the enemy sees an advantage to be gained and makes no effort to secure it, the soldiers are exhausted.

paragraphs.text: 32. If birds gather on any spot, it is unoccupied. Clamour by night betokens nervousness.

sentences.text: If birds gather on any spot, it is unoccupied.
Clamour by night betokens nervousness.

paragraphs.text: 33. If there is disturbance in the camp, the general’s authority is weak. If the banners and flags are shifted about, sedition is afoot. If the officers are angry, it means that the men are weary.

sentences.text: If there is disturbance in the camp, the general’s authority is weak.
If the banners and flags are shifted about, sedition is afoot.
If the officers are angry, it means that the men are weary.

paragraphs.text: 34. When an army feeds its horses with grain and kills its cattle for food, and when the men do not hang their cooking-pots over the camp-fires, showing that they will not return to their tents, you may know that they are determined to fight to the death.

sentences.text: When an army feeds its horses with grain and kills its cattle for food, and when the men do not hang their cooking-pots over the camp-fires, showing that they will not return to their tents, you may know that they are determined to fight to the death.

paragraphs.text: 35. The sight of men whispering together in small knots or speaking in subdued tones points to disaffection amongst the rank and file.

sentences.text: The sight of men whispering together in small knots or speaking in subdued tones points to disaffection amongst the rank and file.

paragraphs.text: 36. Too frequent rewards signify that the enemy is at the end of his resources; too many punishments betray a condition of dire distress.

sentences.text: Too frequent rewards signify that the enemy is at the end of his resources; too many punishments betray a condition of dire distress.

paragraphs.text: 37. To begin by bluster, but afterwards to take fright at the enemy’s numbers, shows a supreme lack of intelligence.

sentences.text: To begin by bluster, but afterwards to take fright at the enemy’s numbers, shows a supreme lack of intelligence.

paragraphs.text: 38. When envoys are sent with compliments in their mouths, it is a sign that the enemy wishes for a truce.

sentences.text: When envoys are sent with compliments in their mouths, it is a sign that the enemy wishes for a truce.

paragraphs.text: 39. If the enemy’s troops march up angrily and remain facing ours for a long time without either joining battle or taking themselves off again, the situation is one that demands great vigilance and circumspection.

sentences.text: If the enemy’s troops march up angrily and remain facing ours for a long time without either joining battle or taking themselves off again, the situation is one that demands great vigilance and circumspection.

paragraphs.text: 40. If our troops are no more in number than the enemy, that is amply sufficient; it only means that no direct attack can be made. What we can do is simply to concentrate all our available strength, keep a close watch on the enemy, and obtain reinforcements.

sentences.text: If our troops are no more in number than the enemy, that is amply sufficient; it only means that no direct attack can be made.
What we can do is simply to concentrate all our available strength, keep a close watch on the enemy, and obtain reinforcements.

paragraphs.text: 41. He who exercises no forethought but makes light of his opponents is sure to be captured by them.

sentences.text: He who exercises no forethought but makes light of his opponents is sure to be captured by them.

paragraphs.text: 42. If soldiers are punished before they have grown attached to you, they will not prove submissive; and, unless submissive, then will be practically useless. If, when the soldiers have become attached to you, punishments are not enforced, they will still be useless.

sentences.text: If soldiers are punished before they have grown attached to you, they will not prove submissive; and, unless submissive, then will be practically useless.
If, when the soldiers have become attached to you, punishments are not enforced, they will still be useless.

paragraphs.text: 43. Therefore soldiers must be treated in the first instance with humanity, but kept under control by means of iron discipline. This is a certain road to victory.

sentences.text: Therefore soldiers must be treated in the first instance with humanity, but kept under control by means of iron discipline.
This is a certain road to victory.

paragraphs.text: 44. If in training soldiers commands are habitually enforced, the army will be well-disciplined; if not, its discipline will be bad.

sentences.text: If in training soldiers commands are habitually enforced, the army will be well-disciplined; if not, its discipline will be bad.

paragraphs.text: 45. If a general shows confidence in his men but always insists on his orders being obeyed, the gain will be mutual.

sentences.text: If a general shows confidence in his men but always insists on his orders being obeyed, the gain will be mutual.

paragraphs.text: 1. Sun Tzŭ said: We may distinguish six kinds of terrain, to wit: (1) Accessible ground; (2) entangling ground; (3) temporising ground; (4) narrow passes; (5) precipitous heights; (6) positions at a great distance from the enemy.

sentences.text: Sun Tzŭ said: We may distinguish six kinds of terrain, to wit: (1) Accessible ground; (2) entangling ground; (3) temporising ground; (4) narrow passes; (5) precipitous heights; (6) positions at a great distance from the enemy.

paragraphs.text: 2. Ground which can be freely traversed by both sides is called accessible.

sentences.text: Ground which can be freely traversed by both sides is called accessible.

paragraphs.text: 3. With regard to ground of this nature, be before the enemy in occupying the raised and sunny spots, and carefully guard your line of supplies. Then you will be able to fight with advantage.

sentences.text: With regard to ground of this nature, be before the enemy in occupying the raised and sunny spots, and carefully guard your line of supplies.
Then you will be able to fight with advantage.

paragraphs.text: 4. Ground which can be abandoned but is hard to re-occupy is called entangling.

sentences.text: Ground which can be abandoned but is hard to re-occupy is called entangling.

paragraphs.text: 5. From a position of this sort, if the enemy is unprepared, you may sally forth and defeat him. But if the enemy is prepared for your coming, and you fail to defeat him, then, return being impossible, disaster will ensue.

sentences.text: From a position of this sort, if the enemy is unprepared, you may sally forth and defeat him.
But if the enemy is prepared for your coming, and you fail to defeat him, then, return being impossible, disaster will ensue.

paragraphs.text: 6. When the position is such that neither side will gain by making the first move, it is called temporising ground.

sentences.text: When the position is such that neither side will gain by making the first move, it is called temporising ground.

paragraphs.text: 7. In a position of this sort, even though the enemy should offer us an attractive bait, it will be advisable not to stir forth, but rather to retreat, thus enticing the enemy in his turn; then, when part of his army has come out, we may deliver our attack with advantage.

sentences.text: In a position of this sort, even though the enemy should offer us an attractive bait, it will be advisable not to stir forth, but rather to retreat, thus enticing the enemy in his turn; then, when part of his army has come out, we may deliver our attack with advantage.

paragraphs.text: 8. With regard to narrow passes, if you can occupy them first, let them be strongly garrisoned and await the advent of the enemy.

sentences.text: With regard to narrow passes, if you can occupy them first, let them be strongly garrisoned and await the advent of the enemy.

paragraphs.text: 9. Should the enemy forestall you in occupying a pass, do not go after him if the pass is fully garrisoned, but only if it is weakly garrisoned.

sentences.text: Should the enemy forestall you in occupying a pass, do not go after him if the pass is fully garrisoned, but only if it is weakly garrisoned.

paragraphs.text: 10. With regard to precipitous heights, if you are beforehand with your adversary, you should occupy the raised and sunny spots, and there wait for him to come up.

sentences.text: With regard to precipitous heights, if you are beforehand with your adversary, you should occupy the raised and sunny spots, and there wait for him to come up.

paragraphs.text: 11. If the enemy has occupied them before you, do not follow him, but retreat and try to entice him away.

sentences.text: If the enemy has occupied them before you, do not follow him, but retreat and try to entice him away.

paragraphs.text: 12. If you are situated at a great distance from the enemy, and the strength of the two armies is equal, it is not easy to provoke a battle, and fighting will be to your disadvantage.

sentences.text: If you are situated at a great distance from the enemy, and the strength of the two armies is equal, it is not easy to provoke a battle, and fighting will be to your disadvantage.

paragraphs.text: 13. These six are the principles connected with Earth. The general who has attained a responsible post must be careful to study them.

sentences.text: These six are the principles connected with Earth.
The general who has attained a responsible post must be careful to study them.

paragraphs.text: 14. Now an army is exposed to six several calamities, not arising from natural causes, but from faults for which the general is responsible. These are: (1) Flight; (2) insubordination; (3) collapse; (4) ruin; (5) disorganisation; (6) rout.

sentences.text: Now an army is exposed to six several calamities, not arising from natural causes, but from faults for which the general is responsible.
These are: (1) Flight; (2) insubordination; (3) collapse; (4) ruin; (5) disorganisation; (6) rout.

paragraphs.text: 15. Other conditions being equal, if one force is hurled against another ten times its size, the result will be the flight of the former.

sentences.text: Other conditions being equal, if one force is hurled against another ten times its size, the result will be the flight of the former.

paragraphs.text: 16. When the common soldiers are too strong and their officers too weak, the result is insubordination. When the officers are too strong and the common soldiers too weak, the result is collapse.

sentences.text: When the common soldiers are too strong and their officers too weak, the result is insubordination.
When the officers are too strong and the common soldiers too weak, the result is collapse.

paragraphs.text: 17. When the higher officers are angry and insubordinate, and on meeting the enemy give battle on their own account from a feeling of resentment, before the commander-in-chief can tell whether or no he is in a position to fight, the result is ruin.

sentences.text: When the higher officers are angry and insubordinate, and on meeting the enemy give battle on their own account from a feeling of resentment, before the commander-in-chief can tell whether or no he is in a position to fight, the result is ruin.

paragraphs.text: 18. When the general is weak and without authority; when his orders are not clear and distinct; when there are no fixed duties assigned to officers and men, and the ranks are formed in a slovenly haphazard manner, the result is utter disorganisation.

sentences.text: When the general is weak and without authority; when his orders are not clear and distinct; when there are no fixed duties assigned to officers and men, and the ranks are formed in a slovenly haphazard manner, the result is utter disorganisation.

paragraphs.text: 19. When a general, unable to estimate the enemy’s strength, allows an inferior force to engage a larger one, or hurls a weak detachment against a powerful one, and neglects to place picked soldiers in the front rank, the result must be a rout.

sentences.text: When a general, unable to estimate the enemy’s strength, allows an inferior force to engage a larger one, or hurls a weak detachment against a powerful one, and neglects to place picked soldiers in the front rank, the result must be a rout.

paragraphs.text: 20. These are six ways of courting defeat, which must be carefully noted by the general who has attained a responsible post.

sentences.text: These are six ways of courting defeat, which must be carefully noted by the general who has attained a responsible post.

paragraphs.text: 21. The natural formation of the country is the soldier’s best ally; but a power of estimating the adversary, of controlling the forces of victory, and of shrewdly calculating difficulties, dangers and distances, constitutes the test of a great general.

sentences.text: The natural formation of the country is the soldier’s best ally; but a power of estimating the adversary, of controlling the forces of victory, and of shrewdly calculating difficulties, dangers and distances, constitutes the test of a great general.

paragraphs.text: 22. He who knows these things, and in fighting puts his knowledge into practice, will win his battles. He who knows them not, nor practises them, will surely be defeated.

sentences.text: He who knows these things, and in fighting puts his knowledge into practice, will win his battles.
He who knows them not, nor practises them, will surely be defeated.

paragraphs.text: 23. If fighting is sure to result in victory, then you must fight, even though the ruler forbid it; if fighting will not result in victory, then you must not fight even at the ruler’s bidding.

sentences.text: If fighting is sure to result in victory, then you must fight, even though the ruler forbid it; if fighting will not result in victory, then you must not fight even at the ruler’s bidding.

paragraphs.text: 24. The general who advances without coveting fame and retreats without fearing disgrace, whose only thought is to protect his country and do good service for his sovereign, is the jewel of the kingdom.

sentences.text: The general who advances without coveting fame and retreats without fearing disgrace, whose only thought is to protect his country and do good service for his sovereign, is the jewel of the kingdom.

paragraphs.text: 25. Regard your soldiers as your children, and they will follow you into the deepest valleys; look on them as your own beloved sons, and they will stand by you even unto death.

sentences.text: Regard your soldiers as your children, and they will follow you into the deepest valleys; look on them as your own beloved sons, and they will stand by you even unto death.

paragraphs.text: 26. If, however, you are indulgent, but unable to make your authority felt; kind-hearted, but unable to enforce your commands; and incapable, moreover, of quelling disorder: then your soldiers must be likened to spoilt children; they are useless for any practical purpose.

sentences.text: If, however, you are indulgent, but unable to make your authority felt; kind-hearted, but unable to enforce your commands; and incapable, moreover, of quelling disorder: then your soldiers must be likened to spoilt children; they are useless for any practical purpose.

paragraphs.text: 27. If we know that our own men are in a condition to attack, but are unaware that the enemy is not open to attack, we have gone only halfway towards victory.

sentences.text: If we know that our own men are in a condition to attack, but are unaware that the enemy is not open to attack, we have gone only halfway towards victory.

paragraphs.text: 28. If we know that the enemy is open to attack, but are unaware that our own men are not in a condition to attack, we have gone only halfway towards victory.

sentences.text: If we know that the enemy is open to attack, but are unaware that our own men are not in a condition to attack, we have gone only halfway towards victory.

paragraphs.text: 29. If we know that the enemy is open to attack, and also know that our men are in a condition to attack, but are unaware that the nature of the ground makes fighting impracticable, we have still gone only halfway towards victory.

sentences.text: If we know that the enemy is open to attack, and also know that our men are in a condition to attack, but are unaware that the nature of the ground makes fighting impracticable, we have still gone only halfway towards victory.

paragraphs.text: 30. Hence the experienced soldier, once in motion, is never bewildered; once he has broken camp, he is never at a loss.

sentences.text: Hence the experienced soldier, once in motion, is never bewildered; once he has broken camp, he is never at a loss.

paragraphs.text: 31. Hence the saying: If you know the enemy and know yourself, your victory will not stand in doubt; if you know Heaven and know Earth, you may make your victory complete.

sentences.text: Hence the saying: If you know the enemy and know yourself, your victory will not stand in doubt; if you know Heaven and know Earth, you may make your victory complete.

paragraphs.text: 1. Sun Tzŭ said: The art of war recognises nine varieties of ground: (1) Dispersive ground; (2) facile ground; (3) contentious ground; (4) open ground; (5) ground of intersecting highways; (6) serious ground; (7) difficult ground; (8) hemmed-in ground; (9) desperate ground.

sentences.text: Sun Tzŭ said: The art of war recognises nine varieties of ground: (1) Dispersive ground; (2) facile ground; (3) contentious ground; (4) open ground; (5) ground of intersecting highways; (6) serious ground; (7) difficult ground; (8) hemmed-in ground; (9) desperate ground.

paragraphs.text: 2. When a chieftain is fighting in his own territory, it is dispersive ground.

sentences.text: When a chieftain is fighting in his own territory, it is dispersive ground.

paragraphs.text: 3. When he has penetrated into hostile territory, but to no great distance, it is facile ground.

sentences.text: When he has penetrated into hostile territory, but to no great distance, it is facile ground.

paragraphs.text: 4. Ground the possession of which imports great advantage to either side, is contentious ground.

sentences.text: Ground the possession of which imports great advantage to either side, is contentious ground.

paragraphs.text: 5. Ground on which each side has liberty of movement is open ground.

sentences.text: Ground on which each side has liberty of movement is open ground.

paragraphs.text: 6. Ground which forms the key to three contiguous states, so that he who occupies it first has most of the Empire at his command, is ground of intersecting highways.

sentences.text: Ground which forms the key to three contiguous states, so that he who occupies it first has most of the Empire at his command, is ground of intersecting highways.

paragraphs.text: 7. When an army has penetrated into the heart of a hostile country, leaving a number of fortified cities in its rear, it is serious ground.

sentences.text: When an army has penetrated into the heart of a hostile country, leaving a number of fortified cities in its rear, it is serious ground.

paragraphs.text: 8. Mountain forests, rugged steeps, marshes and fens—all country that is hard to traverse: this is difficult ground.

sentences.text: Mountain forests, rugged steeps, marshes and fens—all country that is hard to traverse: this is difficult ground.

paragraphs.text: 9. Ground which is reached through narrow gorges, and from which we can only retire by tortuous paths, so that a small number of the enemy would suffice to crush a large body of our men: this is hemmed in ground.

sentences.text: Ground which is reached through narrow gorges, and from which we can only retire by tortuous paths, so that a small number of the enemy would suffice to crush a large body of our men: this is hemmed in ground.

paragraphs.text: 10. Ground on which we can only be saved from destruction by fighting without delay, is desperate ground.

sentences.text: Ground on which we can only be saved from destruction by fighting without delay, is desperate ground.

paragraphs.text: 11. On dispersive ground, therefore, fight not. On facile ground, halt not. On contentious ground, attack not.

sentences.text: On dispersive ground, therefore, fight not.
On facile ground, halt not.
On contentious ground, attack not.

paragraphs.text: 12. On open ground, do not try to block the enemy’s way. On ground of intersecting highways, join hands with your allies.

sentences.text: On open ground, do not try to block the enemy’s way.
On ground of intersecting highways, join hands with your allies.

paragraphs.text: 13. On serious ground, gather in plunder. In difficult ground, keep steadily on the march.

sentences.text: On serious ground, gather in plunder.
In difficult ground, keep steadily on the march.

paragraphs.text: 14. On hemmed-in ground, resort to stratagem. On desperate ground, fight.

sentences.text: On hemmed-in ground, resort to stratagem.
On desperate ground, fight.

paragraphs.text: 15. Those who were called skilful leaders of old knew how to drive a wedge between the enemy’s front and rear; to prevent co-operation between his large and small divisions; to hinder the good troops from rescuing the bad, the officers from rallying their men.

sentences.text: Those who were called skilful leaders of old knew how to drive a wedge between the enemy’s front and rear; to prevent co-operation between his large and small divisions; to hinder the good troops from rescuing the bad, the officers from rallying their men.

paragraphs.text: 16. When the enemy’s men were scattered, they prevented them from concentrating; even when their forces were united, they managed to keep them in disorder.

sentences.text: When the enemy’s men were scattered, they prevented them from concentrating; even when their forces were united, they managed to keep them in disorder.

paragraphs.text: 17. When it was to their advantage, they made a forward move; when otherwise, they stopped still.

sentences.text: When it was to their advantage, they made a forward move; when otherwise, they stopped still.

paragraphs.text: 18. If asked how to cope with a great host of the enemy in orderly array and on the point of marching to the attack, I should say: “Begin by seizing something which your opponent holds dear; then he will be amenable to your will.”

sentences.text: If asked how to cope with a great host of the enemy in orderly array and on the point of marching to the attack, I should say: “Begin by seizing something which your opponent holds dear; then he will be amenable to your will.”

paragraphs.text: 19. Rapidity is the essence of war: take advantage of the enemy’s unreadiness, make your way by unexpected routes, and attack unguarded spots.

sentences.text: Rapidity is the essence of war: take advantage of the enemy’s unreadiness, make your way by unexpected routes, and attack unguarded spots.

paragraphs.text: 20. The following are the principles to be observed by an invading force: The further you penetrate into a country, the greater will be the solidarity of your troops, and thus the defenders will not prevail against you.

sentences.text: The following are the principles to be observed by an invading force: The further you penetrate into a country, the greater will be the solidarity of your troops, and thus the defenders will not prevail against you.

paragraphs.text: 21. Make forays in fertile country in order to supply your army with food.

sentences.text: Make forays in fertile country in order to supply your army with food.

paragraphs.text: 22. Carefully study the well-being of your men, and do not overtax them. Concentrate your energy and hoard your strength. Keep your army continually on the move, and devise unfathomable plans.

sentences.text: Carefully study the well-being of your men, and do not overtax them.
Concentrate your energy and hoard your strength.
Keep your army continually on the move, and devise unfathomable plans.

paragraphs.text: 23. Throw your soldiers into positions whence there is no escape, and they will prefer death to flight. If they will face death, there is nothing they may not achieve. Officers and men alike will put forth their uttermost strength.

sentences.text: Throw your soldiers into positions whence there is no escape, and they will prefer death to flight.
If they will face death, there is nothing they may not achieve.
Officers and men alike will put forth their uttermost strength.

paragraphs.text: 24. Soldiers when in desperate straits lose the sense of fear. If there is no place of refuge, they will stand firm. If they are in the heart of a hostile country, they will show a stubborn front. If there is no help for it, they will fight hard.

sentences.text: Soldiers when in desperate straits lose the sense of fear.
If there is no place of refuge, they will stand firm.
If they are in the heart of a hostile country, they will show a stubborn front.
If there is no help for it, they will fight hard.

paragraphs.text: 25. Thus, without waiting to be marshalled, the soldiers will be constantly on the qui vive; without waiting to be asked, they will do your will; without restrictions, they will be faithful; without giving orders, they can be trusted.

sentences.text: Thus, without waiting to be marshalled, the soldiers will be constantly on the qui vive; without waiting to be asked, they will do your will; without restrictions, they will be faithful; without giving orders, they can be trusted.

paragraphs.text: 26. Prohibit the taking of omens, and do away with superstitious doubts. Then, until death itself comes, no calamity need be feared.

sentences.text: Prohibit the taking of omens, and do away with superstitious doubts.
Then, until death itself comes, no calamity need be feared.

paragraphs.text: 27. If our soldiers are not overburdened with money, it is not because they have a distaste for riches; if their lives are not unduly long, it is not because they are disinclined to longevity.

sentences.text: If our soldiers are not overburdened with money, it is not because they have a distaste for riches; if their lives are not unduly long, it is not because they are disinclined to longevity.

paragraphs.text: 28. On the day they are ordered out to battle, your soldiers may weep, those sitting up bedewing their garments, and those lying down letting the tears run down their cheeks. But let them once be brought to bay, and they will display the courage of a Chu or a Kuei.

sentences.text: On the day they are ordered out to battle, your soldiers may weep, those sitting up bedewing their garments, and those lying down letting the tears run down their cheeks.
But let them once be brought to bay, and they will display the courage of a Chu or a Kuei.

paragraphs.text: 29. The skilful tactician may be likened to the shuai-jan. Now the shuai-jan is a snake that is found in the Ch‘ang mountains. Strike at its head, and you will be attacked by its tail; strike at its tail, and you will be attacked by its head; strike at its middle, and you will be attacked by head and tail both.

sentences.text: The skilful tactician may be likened to the shuai-jan.
Now the shuai-jan is a snake that is found in the Ch‘ang mountains.
Strike at its head, and you will be attacked by its tail; strike at its tail, and you will be attacked by its head; strike at its middle, and you will be attacked by head and tail both.

paragraphs.text: 30. Asked if an army can be made to imitate the shuai-jan, I should answer, Yes. For the men of Wu and the men of Yüeh are enemies; yet if they are crossing a river in the same boat and are caught by a storm, they will come to each other’s assistance just as the left hand helps the right.
